newsitem.title: USA: Refunding seen ending on good note with U.S. 30-yr.
newsitem.headline: Refunding seen ending on good note with U.S. 30-yr.

text.p: Despite two disappointing note auctions this week, U.S. bond traders expect solid demand for Thursday's 30-year auction.
The U.S. Treasury will sell $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT in the third and final leg of its quarterly refunding effort.
"We have a good chance of this being the best of the three auctions," said a head trader at a primary dealership. "There are enough shorts around with the Raytheon deal to properly get this done."
Besides, he added, the market does not have the added weight of another auction tomorrow like the note auctions of the past two days.
The trader was referring to a $3.0 billion, four-tranche corporate debt offering by Raytheon Co that priced shortly before 1100 EDT/1500 GMT.

Both Tuesday's three-year and Wednesday's 10-year note auctions were described as sloppy. But the distribution process has gone rather well so far, with both issues trading with lower yields than their auction levels.
It is too early to tell where the auction will come in, dealers said. In late morning trading, the when-issued 30-year bond was at 6.445 percent, up from 6.43 percent earlier.
Traders figure the issue should be sold at the 6.43-6.44 percent level, which would be at the high of the week. Just last week, it had traded as low at 6.25 percent.
"These bonds look cheap," said one bond trader at a dealer. "They look good on the roll and against the off-the-runs ... There is a chance it may tail, but interest should be good."
Dealers were expected to be the prime buyers of the new bonds, as retail and hedge funds were said to be concerned about the shoddy performance of the market over the past week.
"Customers are not going to buy until the market is in good hands and is headed higher," the bond trader said.
Players said they believed the market will continue its march to higher prices.
"The market is in good shape; it feels pretty good," said a trader at a leading primary dealership, noting solid technical factors.
Another trader added that the 30-year bond would benefit from some projections of a budget surplus as early as next year.
"It's still not a lock we will have a bond auction in November," he said. "I don't care what Treasury officials say."
Officials consistently have denied market speculation that the Department will eliminate the 30-year offering from 1997's final quarterly refunding.
